draft.title: Enlightenment ideas in France
card: The Enlightenment was an 18th century movement that used reason to question traditional authority. In France its writers were called philosophes.
attacked the power and intolerance of the Catholic Church and argued for freedom of speech and religious toleration.
argued in The Social Contract that power comes from the people, so a ruler is legitimate only with the people's consent.
These ideas were spread through books, salons and cafés. They gave critics of absolute monarchy and privilege a way to argue that the old order was unjust.
draft.remember: Philosophes used reason to challenge the king, privilege and the church, and gave critics ideas to argue with.

a.q: Which idea from Rousseau's The Social Contract challenged absolute monarchy?
opts: A ruler's authority depends on the consent of the people
A king rules because he has been chosen by God
Nobles should rule because of their birth and experience
Freedom of the press matters more than who governs
a.why: Rousseau argued that power comes from the people, so a king without their consent has no rightful claim. The divine right claim is the very idea that absolute monarchy relied on, so it is the opposite of his view.
a.clue: Where did Rousseau say a ruler's power comes from?

b.q: A Paris lawyer in 1780 reads Voltaire and begins to criticise church power and religious intolerance. Which statement best describes the effect of such ideas?
opts: They gave critics reasons to question long-held authority
They caused the revolution directly by themselves
They were accepted by the king and his ministers
They were read only by nobles and clergy in Paris
b.why: Enlightenment writing gave critics arguments against traditional authority, including the church. It did not cause the revolution alone: the card says it gave critics a way to argue, not that it forced events. Ideas also spread through books, salons and cafés, not only among nobles.
b.clue: The card says these ideas gave critics something to argue with.

a.best: A ruler's authority depends on the consent of the people

b.best: They gave critics reasons to question long-held authority

problems.detail: The clue ('The card says these ideas gave critics something to argue with') nearly restates the right option, so a student can match the wording without understanding the idea.

proposal.title: Enlightenment ideas in France
card: The Enlightenment was an 18th-century movement that used reason to question traditional authority. In France its writers were called philosophes.
attacked the power and intolerance of the Catholic Church and argued for freedom of speech and religious toleration.
argued in The Social Contract that power comes from the people, so a ruler is legitimate only with the people's consent.

These ideas spread through books, salons and cafés to educated readers beyond the nobles and clergy. They did not cause the revolution on their own, but gave critics of absolute monarchy and privilege arguments that the old order was unjust.
proposal.remember: Philosophes used reason to challenge the king, privilege and the church, and gave critics ideas to argue with.

a.q: Which idea from Rousseau's The Social Contract challenged absolute monarchy?
opts: A ruler's authority depends on the consent of the people
A king rules because he has been chosen by God
Nobles should rule because of their birth and experience
Freedom of the press matters more than who governs
a.why: Rousseau argued that power comes from the people, so a king without their consent has no rightful claim. The divine right claim is the very idea that absolute monarchy relied on, so it is the opposite of his view.
a.clue: Where did Rousseau say a ruler's power comes from?

b.q: A Paris lawyer in 1780 reads Voltaire and begins to criticise church power and religious intolerance. Which statement best describes the effect of such ideas?
opts: They gave critics reasons to question long-held authority
They caused the revolution directly by themselves
They made readers more loyal to the Catholic Church
They were read only by nobles and clergy in Paris
b.why: Enlightenment writing gave people like the lawyer arguments against traditional authority, including the church. It did not cause the revolution on its own: ideas shaped how critics argued, but they did not make events happen by themselves. The ideas also reached educated readers beyond the nobles and clergy.
b.clue: Ideas change how people argue. Can they make events happen alone?
